n1: The node’s criterion is too strict and internally ambiguous: it requires a “recognizably” complete court, while the traces repeatedly treat the absence of a clearly visible full court or floor as decisive. In the edited image, the kitchen is replaced by a basketball setting with a hoop, net, basketballs, and visible court lines/floor; the subject is preserved. Clarify that completion is judged by whether the background reads as a basketball court from the visible combined cues, not whether a full court is shown. Distinguish a basketball-themed backdrop from a court, but do not make full-court visibility an unstated requirement. The four partial judgments versus one complete judgment indicate a criterion-boundary issue, not a transport or dependency failure; high confidence and repeated variation warrant checking that boundary rather than treating them as proof of missing edits. Keep the requested-change check focused on the background and apply the rubric’s partial status only when there is genuine progress that does not meet the clarified completion criterion.

The node’s criterion is too strict and underspecified about what makes a court recognizable: it appears to treat absence of a clearly visible full court as incomplete even when the edited image shows a basketball hoop, ball, and marked court floor. In the supplied edit, the kitchen is replaced by a basketball setting and court markings are visible, so the repeated partial judgments may reflect an overly demanding or ambiguous completeness threshold rather than missing progress. Clarify that the question is whether the background reads as a basketball court from the visible court cues, without requiring a full-court view; distinguish a basketball-themed backdrop from a court using the floor/line evidence. Keep the partial category for genuine progress that still does not establish a court, and assess the whole background rather than requiring every court feature. The traces are valid and queried with no dependency or transport failures; their high confidence alongside repeated disagreement points to criterion calibration, not low-confidence evidence.

The node’s criterion is too strict and underspecified about what makes a background “recognizably a basketball court.” In the edited image, the kitchen is replaced by a basketball setting: a hoop and net, basketballs, and visible court-floor markings are present. The repeated partial judgments appear to discount this combined evidence because a full court is not visible, although the instruction asks for a basketball court background, not a full-court view. Clarify the completion test to assess whether the background as a whole reads as a basketball court from the visible court cues, without requiring an entire court or a particular floor layout. Keep partial for basketball-themed elements that do not establish a court, and distinguish that from this image’s court markings and hoop. The traces are valid and queried with no dependency or transport failures; the disagreement is semantic criterion calibration, not missing evidence. Treat the reference label as an aggregate constraint, not proof by itself.
